title: Number patterns: check every jump
description: A sequence can add, multiply or alternate. Learn to test the rule instead of trusting the first guess.

cover.alt: Wooden blocks arranged in growing rows beside a notebook
cover.credit: AI-generated photorealistic image created for BrainiLab.

practice: Try a few problems at your own pace, then return to any explanation you want to revisit.

sections.title: Write down the changes
sections.html:
Consider 4, 7, 10, 13. The changes are +3, +3 and +3. If the rule says to keep adding three, the next number is sixteen. Checking the gaps gives a reason for the answer.

Compare 3, 6, 12, 24. The gaps are not constant, but each number is twice the previous one. The next number under that rule is forty-eight. Addition and multiplication describe different changes.

sections.title: Try it yourself
sections.html:
Choose a rule and reveal one term at a time. The activity displays the rule so that you can check what it predicts. Try the constant jump first, then doubling, then alternating jumps.

For an alternating +2, +5 rule starting at 1, the terms are 1, 3, 8, 10, 15. Keep track of which jump comes next. Using +2 every time would explain the first change but fail at the second.

sections.title: Short lists do not prove a unique rule
sections.html:
A few numbers do not uniquely determine every future term. Many different rules can fit a short beginning. Puzzle questions often ask for a simple intended rule, but that is a convention, not a mathematical guarantee.

In these exercises, the rule family is stated or the explanation identifies the intended rule. If two answer options genuinely fit the stated conditions, the question needs improving rather than blaming the player.

sections.title: Use a scratch line
sections.html:
Write the numbers on one line and the changes underneath. For multiplication, compare ratios instead of differences. If a rule alternates, mark its two steps separately.

The habit is simple: propose, check, predict. First propose a rule, then check all available steps, and only then use it to predict the next term. This also helps with visual patterns.

questions.prompt: Does a short list of numbers always prove one unique continuation?
options: Only if all terms are even
questions.explanation: Several rules can fit the same short list; the stated rule or conditions matter.
